title: ops-preflight check catalog
description: One shape for all three layers: the engine base (scripts/checks.json), a stack profile (scripts/profiles/<stack>.json) and a repo's override (<repo>/.claude/ops-preflight-profile.json). A profile adds `profile` and `when`; the base has neither. Layers merge by `id`, later wins, so a profile entry may carry nothing but `id` and the field it is replacing. This schema is the readable contract; inspect.sh is the enforced one.

profile.description: Names a STACK, never a product. A product-shaped check belongs in the repo's own override file, not in the engine.

when.description: Present only on a stack profile. The profile loads when this matches the repo. Every matching profile loads; they are additive, not exclusive.

id.description: Stable. The issue title and the answers-file key both derive from it, so renaming one orphans every issue already filed against it.

consumer.description: Which capability or plugin breaks without this. The report groups on it. Required on a NEW check; omitted on a profile entry that only overrides `detect`.

action.description: Optional. The catalog action that breaks, printed beside the consumer.

severity.description: `blocking` — the consumer capability cannot be written without it. `quality` — the loops run, the output is worse. There is no third level and no score.

section.description: Which of the nine headings on the source checklist (AI Ops — Preparing your Harness for Automation) this check belongs to. Required on every check, including a profile entry that only overrides `detect` — the report groups on it independent of `consumer`.

why.description: One line, printed in the report and in the filed issue. Say what breaks, not that the item is good practice.

detect.description: Optional. Absent means no file can answer this and only a human can.

whole_product.description: Optional, defaults false. Marks a check whose QUESTION is about the whole product, not one stack (verify-build-command, verify-test-command, verify-lint-command, verify-warnings-clean). It changes nothing when zero or one stack profile is active for a repo. When TWO OR MORE stack profiles are active, inspect.sh requires a STRONG match tagged to EVERY active stack before resolving `present`: a strong match from only one active stack (a real npm test script, with the dotnet side offering only weak *.csproj evidence) is exactly the false pass this flag exists to stop, because it proves the check for one stack, never the whole product. A strong match with no stack tag at all (a literal root `build.sh`, `test.sh` or `lint.sh`) counts for every active stack at once, since a real repo-wide command genuinely answers the question regardless of how many stacks exist. Falling short downgrades the check to `unknown` (source `partial`) and the report names which active stack has no strong evidence, rather than staying silent about which half of a dual-stack repo was never actually checked.

signal.description: Optional, defaults false. Sets the DEFAULT strength of every pattern in this check's `detect` block to `weak` instead of the normal default of `strong`, without writing `strength: weak` on each one. Use it only for a check where NO evidence could ever be strong — no file can prove the positive fact, it can only hint that the fact might not hold (a NuGet.config hints a restore might need a credential; nothing detectable proves it does not). Where a check's patterns are a genuine MIX — some name the job directly, some are only generic or keyword evidence — prefer marking the individual patterns' own `strength` instead of this flag, so evidence quality is a property of the pattern a reader can see on the pattern, not a check-wide switch. A `strength: strong` on an individual pattern always overrides this flag's `weak` default for that one pattern. A signal check MUST carry an `ask` — without one nothing could ever resolve it, and inspect.sh rejects it.

ask.description: Optional. Absent means report it and never interview on it — for checks where a miss is worth showing but not worth a question.

detect.description: Matches when ANY rule matches. Deliberately tiny: detection is a seed, not an authority.

any_path.description: Globs matched against the whole repo-relative path. `*` matches any characters INCLUDING `/`, so `*.sln` finds one at any depth and `scripts/build*` is anchored at the root. There is no `**`. A bare string carries the default strength (see `path_pattern`); write the object form only to set a glob's strength explicitly.

pattern.description: An extended regular expression, as grep -E reads it.

strength.description: How much a MATCHED pattern proves. STRONG means the matched thing is named for, or dedicated to, the exact job this check is asking about (a script literally named for the job, a skill directory named for it, a canonical single-purpose file) — a match resolves the check straight to `present`, evidence shown, no question. WEAK means the match is only generic or keyword evidence: it proves something exists without proving it does THIS job (a broad-purpose manifest that happens to hold the fact among many others, a keyword found inside a file whose whole purpose is something else, a CI config file that proves CI exists but not that IT publishes) — a match stays `unknown` and still asks, exactly as a `signal` check does today, but keeps the evidence so the question opens with what was found. Optional on an `any_path` object entry and on an `any_file_contains` entry; defaults to `strong`, or to `weak` if the check itself is `signal: true` (see `signal`).

path_pattern.description: One entry in `any_path`. A bare string is a glob at the default strength (`strong`, or `weak` under a `signal: true` check). Use the object form only to set a glob's strength explicitly — most commonly to mark a generically-named or keyword-only glob `weak` inside a check that is otherwise not `signal`.

glob.description: Same glob rules as a bare any_path string.
